intro: Time is money, so let's not waste it: in that one sentence, time is treated like rupiah that you can spend, save or waste. Today you'll see how English thinks in pictures (metaphors), why a pun makes people groan and laugh at the same time, and what people mean when they call something a Trojan horse or an Achilles' heel. Warm-up: think of an Indonesian expression like buaya darat or kambing hitam. How would you explain it to a foreign colleague?
teachingNotes: Recap in one line, don't re-teach: in c1-idioms the learner met idioms as fixed phrases (cut corners, pay off), learnt not to translate Indonesian idioms word for word and met a few twins (air mata buaya = crocodile tears, kambing hitam = a scapegoat, besar kepala = big-headed); in c1-connotation they learnt that words carry a positive, neutral or negative feeling. New here: the system behind idioms. Figurative language (bahasa kiasan) = words used for a picture, not their dictionary meaning. Simile (perumpamaan: like / as ... as: as busy as a bee, as cool as a cucumber, like a fish out of water, sleep like a log; ironic: as clear as mud = not clear at all) vs metaphor (says one thing IS another: This office is a zoo). Conceptual metaphors (families of everyday metaphors native speakers don't notice): time is money (spend, save, waste, invest, run out of time; Indonesian shares it: buang waktu), argument is war (attack a position, defend a claim, shoot down an idea, win/lose an argument, on target), ideas are food (half-baked = not thought through, food for thought, digest, hard to swallow, chew it over, raw data).

Other figures of speech, each with a plain Indonesian gloss: personification (benda dibuat seperti manusia: The economy is recovering, My laptop died, The data tells us...), hyperbole (dilebih-lebihkan: I've told you a million times, I'm starving, This bag weighs a ton), understatement (dikecilkan; very British: That's not ideal / a bit of a nuisance about a disaster, not bad = quite good, I've had better days = a terrible day; Indonesian learners often take it literally), metonymy (menyebut sesuatu lewat hal yang dekat dengannya: the White House = the US president and his staff, Downing Street = the UK prime minister's office, Jakarta announced = the Indonesian government; Indonesian news does the same with Istana and Senayan = DPR; Wall Street = the finance industry).

Indonesian traps and the node's common errors. Don't translate Indonesian figurative expressions word for word: panjang tangan is not 'He is long-handed' but light-fingered (or plainly: he steals things); buaya darat is not 'a land crocodile' but a player / a womaniser (US womanizer); makan hati is not 'eat liver' (say it really gets to me / it hurts; note that English 'Eat your heart out!' is something else: a joking boast, 'be jealous'). Twins and cousins: kambing hitam = a scapegoat (lucky match; NOT a black sheep = the family member who is a disgrace), naik darah ≈ it makes my blood boil, kutu buku = a bookworm, lintah darat = a loan shark, bagai pinang dibelah dua ≈ like two peas in a pod. Mixed metaphors (metafora campur aduk): 'We need to nip it in the bud before it snowballs out of the water' joins three pictures (a garden: nip in the bud = stop it early; snow: snowball = grow bigger and bigger; the sea: blow out of the water = destroy); correct: 'We need to nip it in the bud before it snowballs.' Keep one picture per sentence.

Humour and wordplay: a pun (permainan kata, like Indonesian plesetan or jokes bapak-bapak; English calls the cheesy kind dad jokes) uses one word with two meanings (I used to be a banker, but I lost interest: interest = minat / bunga bank) or two words that sound the same (homophones: two / too, tale / tail). Explain why a joke is funny plainly: the set-up makes you think of one meaning, the punchline (kalimat penutup) switches to the other; the normal reaction to a pun is a groan and a smile. Headlines love puns and double meanings (Fireworks Company Fires Manager After Explosive Meeting). Irony and sarcasm (saying the opposite of what you mean: Lovely weather! in a storm) are shown through context in text; never test them through tone. Don't teach rude double meanings (double entendres); if a learner asks, say they exist and to be careful at work.

Cultural references (allusions: short references to a famous story or person, used without explanation; Indonesian bridge: calling someone a Malin Kundang). Teach with the story in one or two plain sentences and never quote long passages: Achilles' heel (Greek myth: his only weak spot; pronounced a-KIL-eez), a Trojan horse (a 'gift' hiding soldiers; also a type of computer virus), a David and Goliath battle (Bible: small vs giant), a Catch-22 (Joseph Heller's 1961 novel: rules that trap you in a circle: no job without experience, no experience without a job; close to Indonesian buah simalakama, which is any no-win choice), Big Brother (George Orwell's novel Nineteen Eighty-Four, 1949: a power that watches everyone; also the TV show), a Cinderella story (from nobody to success; an underdog team in sport), the elephant in the room (a modern expression, not a story: a big problem nobody mentions), open Pandora's box (start something that releases many problems), a Herculean task (Hercules did twelve impossible jobs), Sherlock (Sherlock Holmes, the detective: 'No kidding, Sherlock' / 'Well done, Sherlock' tease someone for saying something obvious; a ruder version with a swear word exists, not for work).

At C2 every structure is available; the point is understanding and choice. Much of figurative language is style: accept reasonable alternatives (a player / a womaniser / a ladies' man; wasted / lost time) and only mark clear cases wrong: a word-for-word Indonesian translation, a mixed metaphor, a misread double meaning, an allusion used with the wrong meaning. Write original practice jokes and texts; never reproduce real comedy routines, literature or columns. Don't add more allusions unless the learner asks; if they do, give the story in one sentence and the meaning. Flag British vs American where useful (womaniser / womanizer; understatement is especially British).

keyPoints.title: Metaphor, simile and other figures of speech
keyPoints.explanation: A simile compares with like or as ... as (as busy as a bee); a metaphor says one thing is another (This office is a zoo). English is full of everyday metaphor families: time is money (spend, save, waste time), argument is war (attack, defend, shoot down an idea), ideas are food (half-baked, food for thought, digest). Also: personification (The economy is recovering), hyperbole (I've told you a million times), understatement (That's not ideal = it's a disaster) and metonymy (The White House said = the US president's team). Don't translate Indonesian expressions word for word (panjang tangan = light-fingered, not 'long-handed'), and keep one picture per sentence.

examples.en: Her criticism of the budget was right on target.
examples.id: Kritiknya terhadap anggaran itu tepat sasaran.

examples.en: Jakarta has announced new rules for electric scooters.
examples.id: Pemerintah Indonesia telah mengumumkan aturan baru untuk skuter listrik.

examples.en: Lock your drawer: someone on this floor is a bit light-fingered.
examples.id: Kunci lacimu: ada orang di lantai ini yang agak panjang tangan.

id.title: Metafora, simile, dan majas lainnya
id.explanation: Simile (perumpamaan) membandingkan dengan like atau as ... as (as busy as a bee = sibuk sekali); metafora menyatakan sesuatu adalah hal lain (This office is a zoo = kantor ini kacau sekali). Bahasa Inggris penuh dengan 'keluarga' metafora sehari-hari: time is money (spend, save, waste time), argument is war (attack, defend, shoot down an idea), ideas are food (half-baked, food for thought, digest). Ada juga personifikasi (The economy is recovering), hiperbola (I've told you a million times), understatement atau pernyataan yang dikecilkan (That's not ideal = sebenarnya bencana) dan metonimi (The White House said = tim Presiden AS). Jangan menerjemahkan ungkapan Indonesia kata per kata (panjang tangan = light-fingered, bukan 'long-handed'), dan pakai satu gambaran saja dalam satu kalimat.

keyPoints.title: Puns and double meanings
keyPoints.explanation: A pun is a joke built on a word with two meanings (I used to be a banker, but I lost interest: interest = minat and bunga bank) or on two words that sound the same (homophones: two / too). The set-up makes you think of one meaning; the punchline switches to the other. To get the joke, find the word that works both ways. Headlines use the same trick. The normal reaction to a pun is a groan and a smile.

examples.en: I used to be a banker, but I lost interest.
examples.id: Dulu aku bankir, tapi aku kehilangan minat (dan bunga bank).

examples.en: The bike couldn't stand up on its own: it was two tired.
examples.id: Sepedanya tidak bisa berdiri sendiri: ia terlalu lelah (two = dua, too = terlalu: bunyinya sama).

examples.en: Rina's new job at the gym is working out well.
examples.id: Pekerjaan baru Rina di pusat kebugaran berjalan baik (working out = berjalan baik / berolahraga).

id.title: Pun dan makna ganda
id.explanation: Pun (permainan kata, mirip plesetan) adalah lelucon yang memakai kata dengan dua arti (I used to be a banker, but I lost interest: interest = minat dan juga bunga bank) atau dua kata yang bunyinya sama (homofon: two / too). Bagian awal lelucon membuatmu memikirkan satu arti; kalimat penutupnya (punchline) berbelok ke arti yang lain. Untuk menangkap leluconnya, cari kata yang berlaku dua arah. Judul berita juga sering memakai trik ini. Reaksi yang biasa untuk pun: mengeluh 'aduh...' sambil tersenyum.

keyPoints.title: Cultural references (allusions)
keyPoints.explanation: An allusion is a short reference to a famous story or person that the speaker expects you to know. English draws on Greek myths (Achilles' heel = the one weak spot; a Trojan horse = something harmful disguised as a gift; open Pandora's box = start many problems; a Herculean task = a huge, hard job), the Bible (a David and Goliath battle = small vs giant), fairy tales (a Cinderella story = from nobody to success), novels (a Catch-22 = rules that trap you in a circle; Big Brother = a power that watches everyone) and detective stories ('No kidding, Sherlock' = teasing someone who states the obvious). The elephant in the room = a big problem nobody mentions.

examples.en: Public speaking is my Achilles' heel.
examples.id: Berbicara di depan umum adalah titik lemahku.

examples.en: Merging the two ministries' databases will be a Herculean task.
examples.id: Menggabungkan basis data kedua kementerian akan menjadi tugas yang luar biasa berat.

examples.en: Nobody mentioned the budget cuts: they were the elephant in the room.
examples.id: Tidak ada yang menyinggung pemotongan anggaran: itu masalah besar yang semua orang hindari.

id.title: Referensi budaya (alusi)
id.explanation: Alusi adalah rujukan singkat ke cerita atau tokoh terkenal yang dianggap sudah kamu kenal. Bahasa Inggris mengambilnya dari mitos Yunani (Achilles' heel = satu-satunya titik lemah; a Trojan horse = sesuatu yang berbahaya yang menyamar sebagai hadiah; open Pandora's box = memulai sesuatu yang memicu banyak masalah; a Herculean task = tugas yang sangat besar dan berat), Alkitab (a David and Goliath battle = pihak kecil melawan raksasa), dongeng (a Cinderella story = dari bukan siapa-siapa menjadi sukses), novel (a Catch-22 = aturan yang menjebakmu dalam lingkaran; Big Brother = pihak berkuasa yang mengawasi semua orang) dan cerita detektif ('No kidding, Sherlock' = menyindir orang yang menyatakan hal yang sudah jelas). The elephant in the room = masalah besar yang tidak ada yang mau menyinggung.

guidedPractice.prompt: Complete with a 'time is money' verb: 'The client cancelled at the last minute, so we ___ a whole morning preparing for nothing.'
guidedPractice.hint: Time is treated like money. What do you call money you spend for nothing? In Indonesian: buang waktu.

guidedPractice.prompt: Simile or metaphor? 'During the audit week, Bu Ani was as busy as a bee.'
guidedPractice.hint: Look for like or as ... as: a simile compares; a metaphor says one thing IS another.

guidedPractice.prompt: Write the English expression for 'panjang tangan': 'Keep your phone in your bag: one of the new warehouse workers is a bit ___.'
guidedPractice.hint: Not 'long-handed'. In English, a thief's fingers are not long but 'light' (they pick things up easily).

guidedPractice.prompt: Which word carries the double meaning? 'Why are fish so clever? Because they live in schools.'
guidedPractice.hint: A group of fish swimming together is called a school (kawanan ikan).

guidedPractice.prompt: Which reference means 'a huge, very hard job': a Herculean task or a Trojan horse?
guidedPractice.hint: Think of the strong hero from Greek myth who had to do twelve impossible jobs.

independentPractice.prompt: Rewrite this hyperbole as a plain statement: 'I've got a million emails to answer this morning.'
expected: i've got a lot of emails to answer this morning
i have a lot of emails to answer this morning
i've got lots of emails to answer this morning
i have lots of emails to answer this morning
i've got many emails to answer this morning
i have many emails to answer this morning
independentPractice.hint: 'A million' is an exaggeration (hiperbola). Replace it with a plain amount.

independentPractice.prompt: Which word in this headline has two meanings? 'Bakery Owner Rises to the Top of Bandung Business Awards'
independentPractice.hint: What does bread do in the oven? (mengembang)

independentPractice.prompt: A small batik workshop in Solo beats fashion giants from Paris and Milan to win an international design award. Which reference fits: a Cinderella story or Big Brother?
independentPractice.hint: Which story is about someone unknown who suddenly succeeds? Which one is about being watched?

assessment.prompt: Rina's colleague presents a plan to open a new branch in Medan, but he hasn't thought about the costs, the staff or the permits yet. Complete the 'ideas are food' metaphor with ONE word: 'It's an interesting idea, but the plan is still half-___.'
assessment.rubric: Correct: baked (half-baked = setengah matang: not thought through, like bread taken out of the oven too early). Writing the whole word 'half-baked' = 100. 'cooked' or 'done' = 30 (right picture, but not the fixed English expression). 'ready' or 'finished' = 20 (right idea, but no metaphor and not the expression). Small spelling error that keeps the word clear ('bakd') = 80.

assessment.prompt: When the product launch in Surabaya failed, the director blamed Dimas, the newest member of the team, although the real problem was the budget. In Indonesian you'd say: Dimas dijadikan kambing hitam. Complete in English with ONE word: 'Dimas was made the ___.'
assessment.rubric: Correct: scapegoat (= kambing hitam: a lucky match between the two languages). 'black goat' = 0 (word-for-word translation English speakers won't understand). 'black sheep' = 0 (a different meaning: the family or group member who is seen as a disgrace). 'victim' = 30 (partly right, but it loses the meaning of being blamed for others). Small spelling error that keeps the word clear ('scapgoat') = 80.

assessment.prompt: A news headline says: 'Jakarta and Tokyo sign new trade agreement'. Who actually signed the agreement? Write the names of the two countries in English.
acceptableAnswers: the governments of indonesia and japan
the governments of japan and indonesia
the indonesian government and the japanese government
assessment.rubric: Correct: Indonesia and Japan, in either order, or their governments (metonymy: a capital city stands for its government, like 'the White House said...' or 'Senayan' for the DPR). Only one country right = 40. 'Jakarta and Tokyo' repeated, or 'the two cities' / 'the mayors of Jakarta and Tokyo' = 0 (the city names stand for the national governments, not the cities). Small spelling error that keeps the names clear ('Japn') = 80.

assessment.prompt: Dimas left his job at a bakery in Bandung. He told his friends: 'I quit because I wasn't making enough dough.' Write the ONE word that makes this a pun (the word with two meanings).
assessment.rubric: Correct: dough (adonan roti, which a baker makes, and, in informal English, money: he wasn't earning enough). 'making' = 30 (it's part of the joke, but it has only one meaning here). 'quit' or 'bakery' = 0. Small spelling error that keeps the word clear ('dogh') = 80.

assessment.prompt: A news website ran this headline: 'Satay Seller Grilled by Food Inspectors'. Write the ONE word with a double meaning.
assessment.rubric: Correct: grilled (satay is grilled = dibakar, and 'to grill someone' = to question them hard and for a long time: diinterogasi). 'satay' = 20 (it sets up the joke but has one meaning). 'inspectors' or 'seller' = 0. Small spelling error that keeps the word clear ('griled') = 80.

assessment.prompt: Complete with a cultural reference from Greek myth (two words): 'The free cleaning app looked like a nice gift for our office computers, but once it was installed, it secretly sent our customer data to strangers. It was a ___ ___.'
assessment.rubric: Correct: Trojan horse (the Greeks hid soldiers inside a wooden horse that Troy accepted as a gift; today: something that looks harmless but brings danger inside, also a type of computer virus). 'Pandora's box' = 30 (it also releases trouble, but the key idea here is a harmful thing disguised as a gift). 'Achilles' heel' = 0 (a weak spot, a different meaning). Small spelling error that keeps it clear ('trojan hourse') = 80.

assessment.prompt: Complete with ONE word (a name from Greek myth): 'Our team is excellent at sales, but slow customer service is our ___ heel: almost every bad review is about it.'
assessment.rubric: Correct: Achilles (Achilles' heel = the one weak spot of someone or something otherwise strong; the hero could be hurt only on his heel). The apostrophe can be missing or written 's. 'Hercules' or 'Pandora' = 0 (different stories and meanings). A recognisable misspelling ('Achiles', 'Akilles') = 80.

material.title: Metaphor, simile and the metaphors English lives by

id.title: Metafora, simile, dan metafora sehari-hari bahasa Inggris

blocks.text:
**Quick recap:** from C1 you know that an **idiom** is a fixed phrase you can't translate word by word (*cut corners*, *pay off*), and that words carry a feeling (**connotation**: *slim* vs *skinny*). Today you'll see the system behind many idioms: **figurative language** (bahasa kiasan) = words used for a picture, not for their dictionary meaning.

- A **simile** (perumpamaan) compares two things with **like** or **as ... as**: *as busy as a bee* (sibuk sekali), *as cool as a cucumber* (tetap tenang di bawah tekanan), *like a fish out of water* (canggung, merasa asing di tempat baru), *sleep like a log* (tidur nyenyak sekali).
- A **metaphor** (metafora) says one thing **is** the other, with no *like*: *This office is a zoo today.* *Pak Hasan is a walking encyclopedia.*

Indonesian does the same: *bagai pinang dibelah dua* ≈ **like two peas in a pod** (the same idea with a different picture: peas instead of a betel nut). **Careful:** a few similes are **ironic** (ironis: they mean the opposite): *as clear as mud* = not clear at all.

id.text:
**Ulasan singkat:** dari C1 kamu tahu bahwa **idiom** adalah frasa tetap yang tidak bisa diterjemahkan kata per kata (*cut corners*, *pay off*), dan bahwa kata membawa 'rasa' (**konotasi**: *slim* vs *skinny*). Hari ini kamu melihat sistem di balik banyak idiom: **bahasa kiasan** = kata yang dipakai untuk sebuah gambaran, bukan untuk arti kamusnya.

- **Simile** (perumpamaan) membandingkan dua hal dengan **like** atau **as ... as**: *as busy as a bee* (sibuk sekali), *as cool as a cucumber* (tetap tenang di bawah tekanan), *like a fish out of water* (canggung, merasa asing di tempat baru), *sleep like a log* (tidur nyenyak sekali).
- **Metafora** menyatakan satu hal **adalah** hal lain, tanpa *like*: *This office is a zoo today.* (Kantor ini kacau sekali hari ini.) *Pak Hasan is a walking encyclopedia.* (Pak Hasan seperti ensiklopedia berjalan: tahu segalanya.)

Bahasa Indonesia juga begitu: *bagai pinang dibelah dua* ≈ **like two peas in a pod** (idenya sama, gambarannya beda: kacang polong, bukan buah pinang). **Hati-hati:** beberapa simile bersifat **ironis** (artinya kebalikannya): *as clear as mud* = sama sekali tidak jelas.

blocks.text:
**Metaphors English lives by.** Some metaphors are so common that native speakers don't even notice them. They come in **families**: one big picture, many words.
- **Time is money:** *spend, save, waste, invest, run out of* time; *The delay cost us a whole day.* Indonesian shares this one: *menghabiskan waktu, membuang waktu*.
- **Argument is war:** *attack* a position, *defend* a claim, *shoot down* an idea (reject it firmly), *win / lose* an argument, *Her criticism was right on target.*
- **Ideas are food:** a *half-baked* plan (setengah matang: not thought through), *food for thought* (bahan renungan), *digest* a report (mencerna), *hard to swallow* (sulit diterima atau dipercaya), *chew it over* (memikirkannya pelan-pelan).

Knowing the family helps you understand new expressions: if ideas are food, then **raw** data (data mentah) hasn't been 'cooked' (processed) yet.

id.text:
**Metafora yang 'dihidupi' bahasa Inggris.** Ada metafora yang begitu umum sampai penutur asli tidak menyadarinya. Metafora ini datang dalam **keluarga**: satu gambaran besar, banyak kata.
- **Time is money (waktu adalah uang):** *spend, save, waste, invest, run out of* time (menghabiskan, menghemat, membuang, menginvestasikan, kehabisan waktu); *The delay cost us a whole day.* (Keterlambatan itu 'merugikan' kami sehari penuh.) Bahasa Indonesia juga punya: *menghabiskan waktu, membuang waktu*.
- **Argument is war (berdebat itu berperang):** *attack* a position (menyerang pendapat), *defend* a claim (membela klaim), *shoot down* an idea (menolak ide dengan tegas, seperti menembak jatuh pesawat), *win / lose* an argument (menang / kalah berdebat), *Her criticism was right on target.* (Kritiknya tepat sasaran.)
- **Ideas are food (ide itu makanan):** a *half-baked* plan (rencana setengah matang: belum dipikirkan matang), *food for thought* (bahan renungan), *digest* a report (mencerna laporan), *hard to swallow* (sulit diterima atau dipercaya), *chew it over* (memikirkannya pelan-pelan).

Kalau kamu tahu keluarganya, kamu bisa memahami ungkapan baru: kalau ide itu makanan, maka data **raw** (data mentah) belum 'dimasak' (belum diolah).

rows.en: The meeting ran an hour over, so we wasted the whole afternoon.
rows.id: Rapatnya molor satu jam, jadi kami membuang seluruh sore.
rows.note: time is money: wasted, like money

id.note: time is money: wasted, seperti uang yang terbuang

rows.en: The opposition attacked every point in the minister's speech.
rows.id: Pihak oposisi menyerang setiap poin dalam pidato menteri.

rows.en: Dr. Wulan defended her claim with new survey data.
rows.id: Dr. Wulan membela klaimnya dengan data survei baru.

rows.en: The report is eighty pages long: give me a day to digest it.
rows.id: Laporannya delapan puluh halaman: beri aku sehari untuk mencernanya.

rows.en: Sari stayed as cool as a cucumber when the projector broke in the middle of her pitch.
rows.id: Sari tetap tenang sekali waktu proyektornya rusak di tengah presentasinya.

options: My boss is like a volcano when we miss a deadline.
My boss attacked my plan in the meeting.
blocks.explain: A simile compares with like or as ... as: 'like a volcano'. 'My boss is a volcano' is a metaphor (it says he IS one). 'attacked my plan' is also a metaphor, from the 'argument is war' family.

id.explain: Simile membandingkan dengan like atau as ... as: 'like a volcano'. 'My boss is a volcano' adalah metafora (menyatakan dia ADALAH gunung berapi). 'attacked my plan' juga metafora, dari keluarga 'argument is war'.

blocks.text:
Four more **figures of speech** (majas) you meet every day in English:
- **Personification** (personifikasi): a thing is described as if it were a person. *The economy is recovering.* *My laptop died.* *The data tells us that sales are falling.* *Jakarta never sleeps.*
- **Hyperbole** (hiperbola, said 'hai-PER-bo-li'): a huge exaggeration that nobody takes literally. *I've told you a million times.* *I'm starving.* *This suitcase weighs a ton.*
- **Understatement** (pernyataan yang sengaja dikecilkan): the opposite of hyperbole, and very **British**. *That's not ideal* or *a bit of a nuisance* about a flood = it's a disaster. *Not bad* = quite good. *I've had better days* = today was terrible.
- **Metonymy** (metonimi): naming something through a thing closely connected to it. *The White House said...* = the US president and his staff. *Downing Street* = the UK prime minister's office. *Jakarta announced...* = the Indonesian government. *Wall Street* = the American finance industry.

id.text:
Empat **majas** lain yang kamu temui setiap hari dalam bahasa Inggris:
- **Personification** (personifikasi): benda digambarkan seolah-olah manusia. *The economy is recovering.* (Ekonomi sedang pulih.) *My laptop died.* (Laptopku 'mati'.) *The data tells us that sales are falling.* (Data 'memberi tahu' kita bahwa penjualan turun.) *Jakarta never sleeps.* (Jakarta tidak pernah tidur.)
- **Hyperbole** (hiperbola, dibaca 'hai-PER-bo-li'): melebih-lebihkan secara besar-besaran, dan tidak ada yang menganggapnya harfiah. *I've told you a million times.* (Sudah sejuta kali kubilang.) *I'm starving.* (Lapar banget.) *This suitcase weighs a ton.* (Koper ini beratnya minta ampun.)
- **Understatement** (pernyataan yang sengaja dikecilkan): kebalikan hiperbola, dan sangat **British**. *That's not ideal* atau *a bit of a nuisance* tentang banjir = sebenarnya bencana. *Not bad* = cukup bagus. *I've had better days* = hari ini buruk sekali.
- **Metonymy** (metonimi): menyebut sesuatu lewat hal yang sangat dekat dengannya. *The White House said...* = Presiden AS dan stafnya. *Downing Street* = kantor Perdana Menteri Inggris. *Jakarta announced...* = pemerintah Indonesia. *Wall Street* = dunia keuangan Amerika.

rows.en: The printer has decided not to work again.
rows.id: Printernya 'memutuskan' untuk tidak mau bekerja lagi.

id.note: personifikasi: printer tidak bisa memutuskan apa pun

rows.en: I've been waiting for this ojek for a hundred years.
rows.id: Aku sudah menunggu ojek ini seratus tahun.

id.note: hiperbola: mungkin hanya lima belas menit

rows.en: The roof leaked onto the server. It's not ideal.
rows.id: Atapnya bocor ke server. Ini 'kurang ideal' (sebenarnya bencana).

rows.id: Kantor Perdana Menteri Inggris menolak berkomentar.

id.note: metonimi: nama jalannya mewakili kantor perdana menteri

blocks.text: **Indonesian bridges and a trap.** Indonesian news uses metonymy too: *Istana* = the president and his staff, *Senayan* = the DPR (the parliament building is in Senayan). Hyperbole is also familiar (*capek banget, mau mati rasanya*). The trap is **understatement**: when a British colleague says *It's a bit of a problem* or *I'm not entirely convinced*, they may mean *It's a serious problem* or *I don't agree at all*. Read the situation, not just the words.

id.text: **Jembatan dari bahasa Indonesia, dan satu jebakan.** Berita Indonesia juga memakai metonimi: *Istana* = presiden dan stafnya, *Senayan* = DPR (gedung parlemennya di Senayan). Hiperbola juga sudah akrab (*capek banget, mau mati rasanya*). Jebakannya ada di **understatement**: kalau rekan kerja dari Inggris bilang *It's a bit of a problem* atau *I'm not entirely convinced*, maksudnya bisa *Ini masalah serius* atau *Saya sama sekali tidak setuju*. Baca situasinya, bukan hanya kata-katanya.

blocks.prompt: After lunch at the new office canteen, a British colleague says it was 'not bad at all'. What does she mean?
options: She thinks the food was quite good.
She thinks the food was terrible.
blocks.explain: 'Not bad (at all)' is understatement: by saying the opposite of 'bad' softly, she means 'good', often 'quite good'. It's a typical British way to praise without sounding too excited.

id.prompt: Setelah makan siang di kantin kantor yang baru, rekan kerja dari Inggris bilang makanannya 'not bad at all'. Apa maksudnya?
id.explain: 'Not bad (at all)' adalah understatement: dengan pelan-pelan menyangkal 'bad', maksudnya 'bagus', sering 'cukup bagus'. Ini cara khas orang Inggris memuji tanpa terdengar terlalu bersemangat.

material.title: Indonesian expressions: twins, cousins and traps

id.title: Ungkapan Indonesia: kembar, sepupu, dan jebakan

blocks.text:
Indonesian is full of figurative expressions too. When you need one in English, check which group it belongs to:
- **Twins** (the same picture): *kambing hitam* = **a scapegoat** (a lucky match), *air mata buaya* = **crocodile tears**, *besar kepala* = **big-headed**, *naik darah* ≈ **It makes my blood boil**.
- **Cousins** (the same idea, a different picture): *kutu buku* = **a bookworm** (a worm, not a louse), *lintah darat* = **a loan shark** (a shark, not a leech), *bagai pinang dibelah dua* ≈ **like two peas in a pod**.
- **Traps** (word for word makes no sense): *panjang tangan* is not 'long-handed' but **light-fingered** (or simply *he steals things*); *buaya darat* is not 'a land crocodile' but **a player** or **a womaniser** (American spelling: *womanizer*); *makan hati* is not 'eat liver': say **It really gets to me** or **It hurts**.

**Careful with false twins:** *kambing hitam* is **not** *a black sheep* (= the family member everyone is ashamed of). And English *Eat your heart out!* has nothing to do with *makan hati*: it's a joking boast meaning 'be jealous'.

id.text:
Bahasa Indonesia juga penuh ungkapan kiasan. Kalau kamu butuh padanannya dalam bahasa Inggris, cek dulu termasuk kelompok mana:
- **Kembar** (gambarannya sama): *kambing hitam* = **a scapegoat** (kebetulan cocok), *air mata buaya* = **crocodile tears**, *besar kepala* = **big-headed**, *naik darah* ≈ **It makes my blood boil**.
- **Sepupu** (idenya sama, gambarannya beda): *kutu buku* = **a bookworm** (cacing, bukan kutu), *lintah darat* = **a loan shark** (hiu, bukan lintah), *bagai pinang dibelah dua* ≈ **like two peas in a pod**.
- **Jebakan** (kalau diterjemahkan kata per kata tidak masuk akal): *panjang tangan* bukan 'long-handed' tapi **light-fingered** (atau langsung saja *he steals things*); *buaya darat* bukan 'a land crocodile' tapi **a player** atau **a womaniser** (ejaan Amerika: *womanizer*); *makan hati* bukan 'eat liver': katakan **It really gets to me** atau **It hurts**.

**Hati-hati dengan kembar palsu:** *kambing hitam* **bukan** *a black sheep* (= anggota keluarga yang dianggap memalukan). Dan *Eat your heart out!* dalam bahasa Inggris tidak ada hubungannya dengan *makan hati*: itu ucapan pamer yang bercanda, artinya 'iri deh kamu'.

rows.en: When the project failed, they made the intern the scapegoat.
rows.id: Waktu proyeknya gagal, mereka menjadikan si anak magang kambing hitam.

rows.en: My brother is a real bookworm: he reads three novels a week.
rows.id: Adikku benar-benar kutu buku: dia membaca tiga novel seminggu.

rows.en: Never borrow from a loan shark: the interest is 30% a month.
rows.id: Jangan pernah meminjam dari lintah darat: bunganya 30% sebulan.

rows.en: The way he talks to junior staff makes my blood boil.
rows.id: Cara dia bicara kepada staf junior bikin aku naik darah.

rows.en: He's charming, but be careful: he's a bit of a player.
rows.id: Dia memang menawan, tapi hati-hati: dia agak buaya darat.

blocks.text: **One picture per sentence.** Mixing two or three metaphors that don't fit together is called a **mixed metaphor** (metafora campur aduk), and it sounds funny by accident. *We need to nip it in the bud before it snowballs out of the water* joins a garden (*nip it in the bud* = cut the bud before the flower opens: stop a problem early), snow (*snowball* = grow bigger and bigger, like a snowball rolling downhill) and the sea (*blow out of the water* = destroy completely). Keep one picture: **We need to nip it in the bud before it snowballs.** Some comedians mix metaphors on purpose for a laugh; in a report or a meeting, don't.

id.text: **Satu gambaran per kalimat.** Mencampur dua atau tiga metafora yang tidak cocok disebut **mixed metaphor** (metafora campur aduk), dan hasilnya terdengar lucu tanpa sengaja. *We need to nip it in the bud before it snowballs out of the water* menggabungkan kebun (*nip it in the bud* = memotong kuncup sebelum bunganya mekar: menghentikan masalah sejak dini), salju (*snowball* = makin lama makin besar, seperti bola salju yang menggelinding) dan laut (*blow out of the water* = menghancurkan total). Pakai satu gambaran saja: **We need to nip it in the bud before it snowballs.** Ada pelawak yang sengaja mencampur metafora supaya lucu; dalam laporan atau rapat, jangan.

blocks.prompt: Which sentence keeps ONE clear picture?
options: We need to nip it in the bud before it snowballs out of the water.
We need to nip it out of the water before it snowballs.
We need to nip it in the bud before it snowballs.
blocks.explain: Nip in the bud (stop it early) and snowball (grow bigger) work together: both are about something small that would grow. 'Out of the water' adds a third picture, the sea, and 'nip it out of the water' isn't an English expression at all.

id.prompt: Kalimat mana yang memakai SATU gambaran yang jelas?
id.explain: Nip in the bud (hentikan sejak dini) dan snowball (makin membesar) cocok dipakai bersama: keduanya tentang hal kecil yang bisa membesar. 'Out of the water' menambah gambaran ketiga, yaitu laut, dan 'nip it out of the water' sama sekali bukan ungkapan bahasa Inggris.

material.title: Puns, double meanings and why a joke is funny

id.title: Pun, makna ganda, dan kenapa sebuah lelucon lucu

blocks.text:
A **pun** (permainan kata) is a joke that plays with a word that has **two meanings**, or with two words that **sound the same** but are spelt differently (**homophones**, kata sebunyi: *two / too*, *tale / tail*). You already know the idea from Indonesian **plesetan** and **jokes bapak-bapak**; English calls the cheesy kind **dad jokes**.

**Why is a pun funny?** A joke has two parts: the **set-up** makes you think of one meaning, and the **punchline** (kalimat penutup) suddenly switches to the other. Your brain has to hold both meanings at once, and that small surprise is the joke. Take *I used to be a banker, but I lost interest.* You first hear *lost interest* as 'stopped being interested' (kehilangan minat); then you remember that banks pay **interest** (bunga bank). Both meanings fit, and that's the pun.

The usual reaction is a **groan** (mengeluh 'aduh...') and a smile: groaning is part of the fun. To 'get' a pun, ask: **which word works in two ways here?**

id.text:
**Pun** (permainan kata) adalah lelucon yang memainkan kata dengan **dua arti**, atau dua kata yang **bunyinya sama** tapi ejaannya beda (**homofon**, kata sebunyi: *two / too*, *tale / tail*). Kamu sudah kenal idenya dari **plesetan** dan **jokes bapak-bapak**; bahasa Inggris menyebut versi yang 'garing' sebagai **dad jokes**.

**Kenapa pun lucu?** Lelucon punya dua bagian: **set-up** (bagian awal) membuatmu memikirkan satu arti, lalu **punchline** (kalimat penutup) tiba-tiba berbelok ke arti yang lain. Otakmu harus memegang dua arti sekaligus, dan kejutan kecil itulah leluconnya. Contoh: *I used to be a banker, but I lost interest.* Awalnya kamu mendengar *lost interest* sebagai 'kehilangan minat'; lalu kamu ingat bahwa bank memberi **interest** (bunga bank). Kedua arti cocok, dan itulah pun-nya.

Reaksi yang biasa adalah **groan** (mengeluh 'aduh...') sambil tersenyum: mengeluh itu bagian dari keseruannya. Untuk 'menangkap' pun, tanyakan: **kata mana yang berlaku dua arah di sini?**

rows.en: I used to be a banker, but I lost interest.
rows.id: Dulu aku bankir, tapi aku kehilangan minat.

rows.en: The bike couldn't stand up on its own: it was two tired.
rows.id: Sepedanya tidak bisa berdiri sendiri: ia terlalu lelah.

id.note: homofon: two (dua ban) / too tired (terlalu lelah); ban = tyre (British), tire (American)

rows.en: Rina's new job at the gym is working out well.
rows.id: Pekerjaan baru Rina di pusat kebugaran berjalan baik.
rows.note: work out = go well / do exercise

rows.en: Fireworks Company Fires Manager After Explosive Meeting
rows.id: Perusahaan Kembang Api Pecat Manajer Setelah Rapat yang Memanas
rows.note: a headline: fire = dismiss / set alight; explosive = very angry / able to explode

id.note: judul berita: fire = memecat / menyalakan api; explosive = sangat panas, penuh amarah / bisa meledak

blocks.text: **Headlines and humour.** British newspapers especially love puns in headlines, so a headline can look strange until you find the double meaning. Two more tips: **irony** and **sarcasm** (saying the opposite of what you mean: *Lovely weather!* in a storm) are very common in British humour; in writing, the situation tells you it's a joke. And some double meanings are rude: if a group laughs at an ordinary-looking sentence, it may be one of those, so be careful repeating it at work.

id.text: **Judul berita dan humor.** Koran Inggris khususnya suka memakai pun di judul, jadi judul bisa terlihat aneh sampai kamu menemukan makna gandanya. Dua tips lagi: **ironi** dan **sarkasme** (mengatakan kebalikan dari maksudmu: *Lovely weather!* saat badai) sangat umum dalam humor Inggris; dalam tulisan, situasinya yang memberi tahu bahwa itu bercanda. Dan ada makna ganda yang kasar atau jorok: kalau sekelompok orang tertawa mendengar kalimat yang tampak biasa, bisa jadi itu salah satunya, jadi hati-hati mengulanginya di kantor.

blocks.prompt: Why is this joke funny? 'Why did the student eat his homework? Because the teacher said it was a piece of cake.'
options: 'A piece of cake' means 'very easy', and it is also a real slice of cake.
Students are often hungry during lessons.
blocks.explain: The teacher meant the idiom: 'a piece of cake' = very easy. The student took it literally, as a slice of cake you can eat. The joke lives in the two meanings of one phrase.

id.prompt: Kenapa lelucon ini lucu? 'Why did the student eat his homework? Because the teacher said it was a piece of cake.'
id.explain: Gurunya memakai idiom: 'a piece of cake' = sangat mudah. Muridnya mengartikannya harfiah, sebagai sepotong kue yang bisa dimakan. Leluconnya ada pada dua arti dari satu frasa.

material.title: Cultural references: from Achilles' heel to Sherlock

id.title: Referensi budaya: dari Achilles' heel sampai Sherlock

blocks.text:
An **allusion** (alusi, kiasan budaya) is a short reference to a famous story, person or event, used **without explanation**. Indonesian works the same way: call an ungrateful son *si Malin Kundang* and every Indonesian understands, but a foreign colleague won't. English allusions come from Greek myths, the Bible, fairy tales and famous novels:
- **Achilles' heel** (said 'a-KIL-iiz') = the one weak spot. His mother dipped baby Achilles in a magic river, holding him by the heel, so only his heel could be hurt.
- **a Trojan horse** = something harmful disguised as a gift. The Greeks hid soldiers inside a wooden horse; Troy pulled it inside the city walls. Also a type of computer virus.
- **open Pandora's box** = start something that releases many problems you can't control. Pandora opened a box (in older versions a jar) and let all the troubles out into the world.
- **a Herculean task** (said 'her-kyu-LII-en') = a huge, very hard job. The hero Hercules had to do twelve impossible jobs.
- **a David and Goliath battle** = a small side against a giant. In the Bible, young David beat the giant Goliath with a stone and a sling.

id.text:
**Alusi** (kiasan budaya) adalah rujukan singkat ke cerita, tokoh atau peristiwa terkenal, dipakai **tanpa penjelasan**. Bahasa Indonesia juga begitu: sebut anak yang durhaka *si Malin Kundang*, dan semua orang Indonesia paham, tapi rekan kerja dari luar negeri tidak. Alusi bahasa Inggris berasal dari mitos Yunani, Alkitab, dongeng dan novel terkenal:
- **Achilles' heel** (dibaca 'a-KIL-iiz') = satu-satunya titik lemah. Ibunya mencelupkan bayi Achilles ke sungai ajaib sambil memegang tumitnya, jadi hanya tumitnya yang bisa dilukai.
- **a Trojan horse** = sesuatu yang berbahaya yang menyamar sebagai hadiah. Pasukan Yunani menyembunyikan tentara di dalam kuda kayu; penduduk Troya menariknya masuk ke dalam benteng kota. Juga nama sejenis virus komputer.
- **open Pandora's box** = memulai sesuatu yang melepaskan banyak masalah yang tak bisa dikendalikan. Pandora membuka sebuah kotak (dalam versi lama: guci) dan semua kesusahan keluar ke dunia.
- **a Herculean task** (dibaca 'her-kyu-LII-en') = tugas yang sangat besar dan berat. Pahlawan Hercules harus menyelesaikan dua belas tugas yang mustahil.
- **a David and Goliath battle** = pihak kecil melawan raksasa. Dalam Alkitab, David muda mengalahkan raksasa Goliat dengan batu dan ketapel.

blocks.text:
More from fairy tales, novels and modern English:
- **a Cinderella story** = someone unknown or poor suddenly becomes successful. In sport, a small team that goes surprisingly far.
- **a Catch-22** = a situation you can't escape because the rules trap you in a circle: *You need experience to get a job, but you need a job to get experience.* From Joseph Heller's 1961 novel *Catch-22*. Close to Indonesian *buah simalakama*, but *simalakama* is any choice where both options are bad; a Catch-22 is about rules that go round in a circle.
- **Big Brother** = a government or organisation that watches everyone too closely. From George Orwell's novel *Nineteen Eighty-Four* (1949); also the name of a reality TV show.
- **the elephant in the room** = a big, obvious problem that everyone avoids mentioning. It isn't from a famous story: it's a modern expression, but it works like one.
- **Sherlock** (Sherlock Holmes, the famous detective in Arthur Conan Doyle's stories): *No kidding, Sherlock* or *Well done, Sherlock* teases someone who has just said something completely obvious. It's sarcastic: the opposite of praise. (A ruder version with a swear word exists; don't use that one at work.)

id.text:
Lebih banyak lagi dari dongeng, novel dan bahasa Inggris modern:
- **a Cinderella story** = seseorang yang tidak dikenal atau miskin tiba-tiba sukses. Dalam olahraga: tim kecil yang melaju jauh secara mengejutkan.
- **a Catch-22** = situasi yang tak bisa kamu hindari karena aturannya menjebakmu dalam lingkaran: *Kamu butuh pengalaman untuk dapat kerja, tapi butuh kerja untuk dapat pengalaman.* Dari novel Joseph Heller tahun 1961, *Catch-22*. Mirip *buah simalakama*, tapi *simalakama* adalah pilihan apa pun yang kedua opsinya buruk; Catch-22 khusus tentang aturan yang berputar-putar.
- **Big Brother** = pemerintah atau organisasi yang mengawasi semua orang secara berlebihan. Dari novel George Orwell *Nineteen Eighty-Four* (1949); juga nama acara reality TV.
- **the elephant in the room** = masalah besar dan jelas yang semua orang hindari untuk dibicarakan. Ini bukan dari cerita terkenal, melainkan ungkapan modern, tapi cara kerjanya sama.
- **Sherlock** (Sherlock Holmes, detektif terkenal dalam cerita Arthur Conan Doyle): *No kidding, Sherlock* atau *Well done, Sherlock* menyindir orang yang baru saja menyatakan hal yang sudah jelas sekali. Ini sarkastis: kebalikan dari pujian. (Ada versi yang lebih kasar dengan kata makian; jangan dipakai di kantor.)

rows.en: Changing one rule could open Pandora's box: every department will want an exception.
rows.id: Mengubah satu aturan bisa membuka kotak Pandora: setiap divisi akan minta pengecualian.

rows.en: A village football team reaching the national final is a real Cinderella story.
rows.id: Tim sepak bola desa yang sampai ke final nasional benar-benar kisah Cinderella.

rows.en: The new app tracks every click we make. It feels a bit Big Brother.
rows.id: Aplikasi baru itu melacak setiap klik kita. Rasanya seperti diawasi terus.
rows.note: used like an adjective in informal English

id.note: dalam bahasa Inggris informal dipakai seperti kata sifat

rows.en: A local coffee chain against a global giant: it's David and Goliath.
rows.id: Jaringan kopi lokal melawan raksasa global: ini David melawan Goliat.

blocks.prompt: 'For new graduates in Jakarta, it's a real Catch-22: ___' Which ending fits?
options: a small start-up beat a huge company to win the contract.
employers want experience, but you can't get experience without a job.
the government watches every application online.
blocks.explain: A Catch-22 is a trap made by rules that go round in a circle: no job without experience, no experience without a job. The first ending is a David and Goliath story; the third is Big Brother.

id.prompt: 'For new graduates in Jakarta, it's a real Catch-22: ___' Akhiran mana yang cocok?
id.explain: Catch-22 adalah jebakan dari aturan yang berputar-putar: tidak ada kerja tanpa pengalaman, tidak ada pengalaman tanpa kerja. Akhiran pertama adalah kisah David dan Goliat; yang ketiga adalah Big Brother.

resources.title: What Is Your Achilles' Heel?
resources.source: VOA Learning English (Words and Their Stories)
resources.note: A short story about where the expression Achilles' heel comes from and how it's used today, with a 5-minute audio version. It also covers one extra expression, head over heels (deeply in love). American English.

id.note: Cerita singkat tentang asal-usul ungkapan Achilles' heel dan cara memakainya sekarang, dengan versi audio 5 menit. Juga membahas satu ungkapan tambahan, head over heels (jatuh cinta setengah mati). Bahasa Inggris Amerika.

id.intro: Time is money, so let's not waste it: dalam satu kalimat itu, waktu diperlakukan seperti rupiah yang bisa dihabiskan, dihemat atau dibuang. Hari ini kamu akan melihat bagaimana bahasa Inggris berpikir lewat gambaran (metafora), kenapa sebuah pun membuat orang mengeluh 'aduh...' sekaligus tertawa, dan apa maksud orang saat menyebut sesuatu a Trojan horse atau an Achilles' heel. Pemanasan: pikirkan ungkapan Indonesia seperti buaya darat atau kambing hitam. Bagaimana kamu menjelaskannya kepada rekan kerja dari luar negeri?
suggestedQuestions: Bisakah saya menerjemahkan peribahasa Indonesia ke bahasa Inggris?
Kenapa orang mengeluh 'aduh...' kalau mendengar pun?
Referensi budaya mana yang sebaiknya saya pelajari dulu?

assessment.fig-1: Rekan kerja Rina mempresentasikan rencana membuka cabang baru di Medan, tapi dia belum memikirkan biaya, staf maupun izinnya. Lengkapi metafora 'ide itu makanan' dengan SATU kata bahasa Inggris: 'It's an interesting idea, but the plan is still half-___.'
assessment.fig-2: Waktu peluncuran produk di Surabaya gagal, direkturnya menyalahkan Dimas, anggota tim paling baru, padahal masalah sebenarnya ada di anggaran. Dalam bahasa Indonesia: Dimas dijadikan kambing hitam. Lengkapi dalam bahasa Inggris dengan SATU kata: 'Dimas was made the ___.'
assessment.fig-3: Sebuah judul berita berbunyi: 'Jakarta and Tokyo sign new trade agreement'. Siapa sebenarnya yang menandatangani perjanjian itu? Tulis nama kedua negaranya dalam bahasa Inggris.
assessment.fig-4: Dimas berhenti dari pekerjaannya di sebuah toko roti di Bandung. Dia bilang ke teman-temannya: 'I quit because I wasn't making enough dough.' Tulis SATU kata yang membuat kalimat ini menjadi pun (kata yang punya dua arti).
assessment.fig-5: Sebuah situs berita memuat judul ini: 'Satay Seller Grilled by Food Inspectors'. Tulis SATU kata yang punya makna ganda.
assessment.fig-6: Lengkapi dengan referensi budaya dari mitos Yunani (dua kata bahasa Inggris): 'The free cleaning app looked like a nice gift for our office computers, but once it was installed, it secretly sent our customer data to strangers. It was a ___ ___.'
assessment.fig-7: Lengkapi dengan SATU kata (sebuah nama dari mitos Yunani): 'Our team is excellent at sales, but slow customer service is our ___ heel: almost every bad review is about it.'
